screens.title: Overview
screens.body:
**Topics covered**

- Long Descriptions for Complex Charts
- Screenshots
- Grouping Objects
- Master Slide and Background Content
- Changing Slide Layouts
- Using Tables Correctly
- Don't Use Color Alone
- Color Contrast
- Designate the Correct Language
- Animation and Transitions
- Video, Audio, and Captions
- Embedded and Copied-In Objects
- Add Benetech's PowerPoint Template to PowerPoint
- Accessible Alternative Formats

**Why this matters**

PowerPoint Basic covers the habits every deck needs. This Advanced module goes further into what comes up in more complex presentations: detailed charts and screenshots, grouped shapes, the slide master and layouts, tables, color, language, animation, video, embedded objects, and accessible formats. A slide built from loose text boxes, a chart with no explanation, or a video with no captions can be just as unusable for someone using a screen reader or with low vision as a deck with no slide titles at all.

It's optional, and recommended if you build more complex or formal presentations - or whenever you'd like to go deeper. Each screen covers one concept: what the problem is, and exactly how to fix it. A short quiz follows once you've been through all of them.

screens.title: Long Descriptions for Complex Charts
screens.body:
A simple photo might only need a sentence of alt text. A chart, graph, or infographic packed with data usually needs more explanation than a screen reader user can absorb from a single alt text field.

**Do:**

- Write a short alt text description as you would for any image - just enough to say what the chart shows.
- {{answer:ppt-q6}}Then put the fuller explanation somewhere else the audience can actually reach it: in nearby text on the slide, in the slide's Notes, or on an appendix slide at the end of the deck.{{/answer}} A table showing the same data the chart displays is often the clearest option.
- If the longer explanation lives somewhere else in the deck, say so in the alt text itself ("see the data table in the Appendix") so a listener knows where to go.

**Don't:** Try to cram a full explanation of a complex chart into the alt text field alone - keep alt text short, and put the detail where it has room to breathe.

screens.title: Screenshots
screens.body:
A screenshot is really just another image, so the same alt text and decorative-vs-meaningful rules from PowerPoint Basic apply - but a screenshot has its own extra wrinkle: text baked into a screenshot (a menu label, an error message, a paragraph of on-screen text) can't be read as text by AT at all, no matter how good the surrounding alt text is.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q29}}When a screenshot's alt text needs to convey more than just what it visually shows - the exact wording of an error message, values typed into a form, the steps in a multi-step dialog - write that text out in the description itself, rather than describing the screenshot only in general terms.{{/answer}}
- Crop a screenshot down to just the relevant portion of the window or screen, and enlarge it if needed - a screenshot shrunk to fit a slide often becomes too small to read even for sighted viewers.
- Consider whether the key information would actually be clearer as real, typed text or a real table on the slide instead of an image of it - a screenshot of a settings dialog is sometimes better replaced by simply listing the two or three settings that actually matter.
- If a screenshot shows a lengthy or complex sequence, use the same long-description approach from the previous screen - a short alt text summary, with the full detail in nearby text, the Notes pane, or an appendix slide.
- {{answer:ppt-q30}}When presenting a screenshot live, say out loud whatever you'd otherwise only point at or highlight on screen - name the specific button, field, or line of text directly ("the Save button in the bottom-right", not just "this button here") - and read aloud the same key on-screen text you already transcribed into the alt text.{{/answer}}

**Don't:** Write alt text for a screenshot that only describes its general appearance ("a screenshot of a dialog box") when the actual text inside it is the entire point of including it.

screens.title: Grouping Objects
screens.body:
This one is specific to PowerPoint: alt text applied to an individual shape often isn't read by assistive technology at all. If a piece of your slide is actually built from several separate shapes - an icon made of overlapping circles, a diagram assembled from boxes and arrows - AT may not pick up any of it.

**Do:** {{answer:ppt-q7}}Select every shape that makes up the visual, group them into a single object (right-click > **Group**, or the **Group** button on the **Shape Format** tab), and add one alt text description to that group{{/answer}} describing the whole thing - including the order and relationship of the pieces inside it, the same way you would for a complex image.

**Don't:** Leave a multi-shape graphic ungrouped and add alt text to its individual pieces, expecting AT to read all of them - group first, then describe the result as one object.

screens.title: Master Slide and Background Content
screens.body:
The Slide Master lets you set a consistent look - colors, fonts, a logo, a footer - across every slide in the deck at once. It's a great accessibility tool for keeping things consistent, with one important catch.

{{answer:ppt-q8}}Text and images placed on the Slide Master itself are never read by assistive technology, no matter how meaningful they are - only content on the actual presentation slide gets announced.{{/answer}}

**Do:**

- If something on the master slide actually conveys meaning (a logo, a revision date, anything more than decoration), add an equivalent on the real slide too - either as visible text, or as a small placeholder image with the same alt text.
- You only need to do this once, on the first slide - repetitive footer-style content doesn't need to be repeated on every single slide after that.

**Don't:** Assume that because a logo or label appears on every slide via the master, AT users are hearing it too - they aren't, unless it also exists on the slide itself.

screens.title: Changing Slide Layouts
screens.body:
A slide's layout - Title Slide, Title and Content, Two Column, Picture with Caption, and so on - decides where its title and content go. Changing it gives a deck its style and keeps an audience's attention, and doing it with PowerPoint's own layouts keeps every slide accessible too.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q32}}Change a slide's look by choosing a different layout (on the **Home** tab of the ribbon, choose **Layout** or **Slide Layout**), not by drawing your own text boxes{{/answer}} - the title and content areas of every layout are real placeholders, which is what assistive technology relies on to find a slide's title and content.
- Put pictures and tables into a layout's placeholders (click the picture or table icon inside the placeholder) so PowerPoint handles their size, spacing, and alignment for you.
- {{answer:ppt-q33}}After changing a layout, review both the reading order (open the Reading Order pane) and the visual placement of everything on the slide{{/answer}} - content moves into the new layout's placeholders, so the order it is read in can change and objects can end up overlapping or out of place. If something does, **Home > Reset** puts the slide's placeholders back to the layout's default positions.

**Don't:** Fix a slide that doesn't fit its layout by laying a text box on top of it. A text box is not a placeholder - it can never serve as the slide's title, and it may be read out of order.

screens.title: Using Tables Correctly
screens.body:
Tables in a slide deck run into the same accessibility issues they do everywhere else in Office - plus, a table often isn't even the best choice on a slide in the first place.

**Do:**

- Consider whether the data could be presented another way first - a short paragraph with a heading is often easier to follow on a slide than a table is.
- If a table is genuinely the right choice, build it with PowerPoint's real **Table** feature (**Insert > Table**), never by pasting a grid of text into a plain text box.
- {{answer:ppt-q13}}Turn on **Header Row** from the **Table Design** tab so column headings are actually marked as headers, not just styled to look bold.{{/answer}}
- Keep the structure simple: one data point per cell, no merged or split cells.

**Don't:** Copy and paste cells directly from an Excel spreadsheet - that usually creates an image or an unstructured block of text instead of a real, readable table.

screens.title: Don't Use Color Alone
screens.body:
Coding a status red for "over budget" and green for "on budget", with no other difference, feels intuitive - but it depends entirely on being able to see and distinguish color. A screen reader never announces color at all, and colorblind audience members may not be able to tell the colors apart either way.

**Do:** {{answer:ppt-q10}}Always pair a color-coded meaning with a second, non-color indicator - a text label, a symbol, or a pattern - so the information doesn't disappear for anyone who can't perceive the color difference.{{/answer}} "Over Budget" written out, or a distinct icon next to each status, works regardless of how someone perceives color.

**Don't:** Use color as the only way to distinguish two things on a slide, whether that's status, importance, or a correct vs. incorrect answer.

screens.title: Color Contrast
screens.body:
Strong contrast between text and its background matters even more on a slide than in a document - it's often read from across a room, or through a screen-share compression, on top of everything low vision or color blindness already affects.

**Do:**

- Use PowerPoint's built-in **Design Ideas** and themes where you can - they're already checked for accessible contrast, which a fully custom background color behind default text usually isn't.
- {{answer:ppt-q11}}Check contrast in charts and graphs too, not just body text - a low-contrast slice color or gridline can be just as unreadable as low-contrast text.{{/answer}}
- Run **Review > Check Accessibility** (covered in PowerPoint Basic) to flag insufficient contrast automatically.

**Don't:** Assume a color combination is fine just because it looks fine on your own monitor - test it, especially anywhere you've moved away from a built-in theme.

screens.title: Designate the Correct Language
Animation and Transitions
screens.body:
Animation can add visual interest, or walk an audience through a multi-step idea one piece at a time - but it needs to be set up carefully to stay usable, and some of it can be genuinely dangerous.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q16}}Set each animation to start **On Click** (Animations tab > Timing pane), not on an automatic delay or a custom trigger{{/answer}} - this lets someone advance at their own pace with either the mouse or the keyboard.
- If a single animated build is hard to make accessible, consider breaking it into several slides instead - one step per slide, each advancing on click.
- Keep transition effects short enough to settle within about five seconds, so AT isn't left trying to read text that's still moving.

**Don't:**

- {{answer:ppt-q17}}Include flashing or blinking content faster than three flashes per second - faster than that can trigger seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy.{{/answer}}
- Rely on PowerPoint's built-in checkbox or form-style controls for interactivity - they're often not reachable by keyboard, and may not be read correctly by screen readers at all.

screens.title: Video, Audio, and Captions
screens.body:
A video embedded in a slide brings its own accessibility needs on top of everything else in this module.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q18}}Add captions or subtitles to the video file itself *before* inserting it into PowerPoint{{/answer}} - PowerPoint can't attach a separate caption file to a video the way some other tools can.
- Provide an audio description track (or narrate the important visual details yourself) for any meaning the video conveys only visually, for viewers who are blind or have low vision.
- Interpret meaningful audio in voice or ASL, matching whichever is the primary language of your audience.

**Don't:** Run **Compress Media** or **Optimize Media Compatibility** on a video and assume its captions survived - both features are known to strip out captions and alternate audio tracks, so re-check the video afterward if you use either one.

screens.title: Embedded and Copied-In Objects
screens.body:
It's common to pull content from another file type - a spreadsheet, a PDF, a document - straight into a slide. Done the wrong way, this can quietly break both keyboard access and how correctly AT reads the result.

**Do:**

- {{answer:ppt-q19}}Use PowerPoint's actual object types for pasted-in content - for example, a real Table object for spreadsheet data - rather than copying it in as a flat image or an unstructured block.{{/answer}}
- If a file truly needs to be embedded (double-clickable to open in its own program), also make that same file available separately, with instructions for how to get it - an embedded object may not be reachable by keyboard or read correctly by AT at all.

**Don't:** Copy content from another file type into a slide without checking what it actually became - a quick visual match to the source file isn't the same as a real, accessible object underneath it.

screens.title: Add Benetech's PowerPoint Template to PowerPoint
screens.body:
Benetech has a master PowerPoint template with accessible layouts, readable text sizes, and clear space at the bottom for captions already set up. Starting every deck from it gives you real title placeholders and a sensible reading order before you have typed a word.

**Do:** {{answer:ppt-q34}}Start each new deck from the Benetech template{{/answer}}. [Download the Benetech PowerPoint template](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/benetech/Accessibility-Training-Modules/main/modules/powerpoint-accessibility-advanced/resources/Benetech-PowerPoint-Template.potx) (it is also in your take-home materials), then use it either of two ways:

**Option 1 - run it from your desktop.** Save the file to your desktop. Whenever you want a Benetech-styled deck, double-click it. If PowerPoint opens it in Protected View, click **Enable Editing** - you get a new, unsaved deck based on the template.

**Option 2 - save it to your Custom Office Templates folder.** Then the template is always there when you start a new deck, with no file to hunt for.

**On Windows:**

1. Copy the folder address: {{copy:Copy Windows folder address|Documents\Custom Office Templates}}
2. Open File Explorer, click its address bar, paste with Ctrl+V, and press Enter. The Custom Office Templates folder opens. If Windows says it cannot find it, the folder does not exist yet: open **Documents**, create a new folder named exactly **Custom Office Templates**, and try again.
3. Move or copy the template file into that folder.
4. In PowerPoint, choose **File > New** and open the **Personal** tab. The Benetech template is there; choose it to start a new deck. If it does not appear right away, close and reopen PowerPoint.
5. If it still is not under Personal, choose **File > Options > Save**. The **Default personal templates location** box shows the folder PowerPoint is looking in - put the file there instead.

**On a Mac:**

1. Close PowerPoint, then copy the folder address: {{copy:Copy Mac folder address|~/Library/Group Containers/UBF8T346G9.Office/User Content.localized/Templates.localized}}
2. In Finder, choose **Go > Go to Folder** (Shift+Command+G), paste with Command+V, and press Return.
3. Move or copy the template file into that folder.
4. Open PowerPoint and choose **File > New from Template**. Open the **Personal** tab, where the Benetech template is, and choose it to start a new deck.

**Don't:** Copy an old deck and delete its content to reuse its look. Slides built that way carry over whatever was wrong with the old deck, and they won't pick up later improvements to the template.

screens.title: Accessible Alternative Formats
screens.body:
Once your deck itself is in good shape, offering it in more than one format gives your audience the option that works best for however they're accessing it.

**Do:**

- When exporting to PDF, use the export option that enables accessibility tagging (for example, checking "Enable accessibility and reflow" in an Acrobat export, or your PDF tool's equivalent) rather than a plain print-to-PDF - {{answer:ppt-q21}}a plain print-to-PDF strips out headings, alt text, and structure the same way it does from Word{{/answer}}.
- If a tagged PDF export isn't available to you, PowerPoint's **Outline View** can be copied into a Word or plain-text document as a fallback - number each slide and paste in its alt text alongside it.

**Don't:** Treat a plain, untagged PDF export as an accessible substitute for the deck - check that headings and image descriptions actually carried over before sharing it.
